concepts.name: Two-Sector Circular Flow Model: Assumptions and Mechanics
key_dimensions: Households as factor owners and firms as producers — the closed loop of factor and product markets
Assumptions: no government, no foreign sector, no savings/investment — a barter-like money economy
Real flow vs. Money flow distinction within the two-sector model
UPSC trap: Why this model represents a 'leakage-free' economy and what breaks this condition

concepts.name: Real Flow vs. Money Flow: Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Real flow: movement of goods, services, and factor inputs (land, labour, capital, enterprise) between sectors
Money flow: corresponding payment streams — wages, rent, interest, profit and expenditure on goods/services
Why both flows are equal in value in a simplified model — the identity of income and output
UPSC trap: Confusing direction of real and money flows; real flows move opposite to money flows

concepts.name: Leakages and Injections: Definitions, Types, and Equilibrium Condition
key_dimensions: Three leakages: Savings (S), Taxes (T), Imports (M) — withdrawals from the circular flow
Three injections: Investment (I), Government Expenditure (G), Exports (X) — additions to circular flow
Equilibrium condition: Total Leakages = Total Injections (S+T+M = I+G+X)
UPSC trap: Leakages do not destroy money — they redirect it; distinguishing leakage from loss

concepts.name: Savings as a Leakage: The Paradox of Thrift
key_dimensions: Individual savings reduce consumption, depressing aggregate demand — Keynesian perspective
Paradox: What is rational for an individual (saving more) can be harmful for the economy collectively
Savings become an injection only when channelled as investment through financial intermediaries
UPSC trap: Savings are not inherently negative — the issue is when savings exceed investment (S > I)

concepts.name: Three-Sector Circular Flow: Role of Government
key_dimensions: Government as a third sector — collects taxes (leakage) and injects government expenditure (G)
Transfer payments (pensions, subsidies) — are they injections? Their treatment in national income accounting
Fiscal policy operates through modifying the G and T components of the circular flow
UPSC trap: Transfer payments are NOT counted in GDP/NI as they don't involve productive activity, yet they affect the flow

concepts.name: Four-Sector Circular Flow: Open Economy and the Role of Foreign Trade
key_dimensions: Exports (X) as injection — foreign demand adds to domestic circular flow
Imports (M) as leakage — domestic expenditure flows out to foreign economies
Net exports (X–M) or trade balance and its effect on the size of circular flow
UPSC trap: Current account deficit means M > X, implying leakages exceed injections from the trade component alone

concepts.name: Factor Markets vs. Product Markets in Circular Flow
key_dimensions: Factor market: firms demand factors (labour, land, capital); households supply them and receive factor income
Product market: households demand goods/services; firms supply them and receive revenue
How national income (measured via factor payments) equals national product (measured via output value)
UPSC trap: Factor income = GDP at factor cost; product market revenue = GDP at market price — reconciliation via net indirect taxes

concepts.name: Financial Intermediaries as Conduit Between Savings and Investment
key_dimensions: Role of banks, capital markets, NBFCs in converting household savings (leakage) into firm investment (injection)
When S > I: deflationary gap — circular flow contracts; when I > S: inflationary gap — flow expands
Role of RBI/monetary policy in influencing this savings-investment channel
UPSC trap: Investment in circular flow means real/physical investment (capital formation), NOT financial investment

concepts.name: Multiplier Effect and its Connection to Circular Flow
key_dimensions: An injection (e.g., government spending) circulates multiple times — income generated exceeds initial injection
Multiplier (k) = 1 / (1 – MPC) = 1 / MPS — derived from the leakage rate
Higher leakages (high MPS, high taxes, high imports) reduce the multiplier value
UPSC trap: Multiplier works in reverse too — a withdrawal/leakage creates a contractionary multiplier effect

concepts.name: Measuring National Income via Three Methods — Rooted in Circular Flow
key_dimensions: Output/Product method: value of goods and services produced — measures the product market flow
Income method: sum of factor incomes (wages + rent + interest + profit) — measures factor market flow
Expenditure method: C + I + G + (X–M) — measures spending injections into the circular flow
UPSC trap: All three methods yield the same result theoretically — discrepancies arise from statistical errors, not conceptual differences

concepts.name: Consumption Function and Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC)
key_dimensions: MPC = ΔC/ΔY — proportion of additional income spent on consumption; keeps money circulating
MPS = 1 – MPC — the leakage rate; higher MPS implies faster withdrawal from circular flow
Autonomous consumption vs. induced consumption and their roles in sustaining the flow
UPSC trap: MPC cannot exceed 1 in Keynesian framework; if MPC = 1, multiplier is infinite (no leakage)

concepts.name: Injection–Withdrawal Equilibrium and Keynesian Income Determination
key_dimensions: Equilibrium national income: where aggregate demand (injections) equals aggregate supply (leakages)
Below-equilibrium: injections > leakages — income expands; above-equilibrium: leakages > injections — income contracts
Graphical representation: 45° line diagram and AD–AS intersection in Keynesian cross
UPSC trap: Keynesian equilibrium may occur below full employment — this is the concept of deflationary gap, requiring fiscal stimulus

concepts.name: Transfer Payments: Exclusion from Circular Flow of Income but Inclusion in Government Budget
key_dimensions: Transfer payments (subsidies, pensions, unemployment benefits) are unilateral — no productive service in return
Excluded from GDP/NI calculations but form a large part of government expenditure
They redistribute existing income rather than creating new income — hence outside the productive circular flow
UPSC trap: Subsidy to a firm that uses it for production DOES enter circular flow indirectly through increased output

concepts.name: Stock vs. Flow Concepts in the Context of Circular Flow
key_dimensions: Flow variables: income, consumption, investment, GDP — measured over a time period
Stock variables: wealth, money supply, capital stock — measured at a point in time
Circular flow represents flows; national wealth is the cumulative stock built from past flows
UPSC trap: Money supply (M1, M2, M3) is a stock; expenditure on goods is a flow — common confusion in MCQs

concepts.name: Inflationary and Deflationary Gaps in the Circular Flow Framework
key_dimensions: Inflationary gap: Aggregate demand exceeds full-employment output — injections > leakages at full employment
Deflationary gap: Aggregate demand falls short of full-employment output — leakages > injections
Policy responses: Contractionary fiscal/monetary policy for inflationary gap; expansionary for deflationary gap
UPSC trap: 'Recessionary gap' and 'deflationary gap' are often used interchangeably but have a technical distinction in some frameworks

concepts.name: Open Economy Circular Flow and Balance of Payments Connection
key_dimensions: Current account captures trade in goods/services (X–M leakage/injection dynamic)
Capital account captures financial flows — FDI, FPI inflows are injections; outflows are leakages
A current account deficit must be financed by capital account surplus — circular flow perspective on BOP
UPSC trap: Capital account surplus (foreign investment inflow) appears as injection but creates future income leakage via profit repatriation

concepts.name: Role of Money in Circular Flow: Medium of Exchange vs. Hoarding
key_dimensions: Money facilitates circular flow by acting as a medium — velocity of money affects the size of effective flow
Hoarding (keeping money idle) is a leakage even before reaching the formal savings channel — reduces velocity
Quantity Theory of Money (MV = PQ) — V (velocity) directly relates to the speed of circular flow
UPSC trap: In a barter economy, circular flow exists (real flow) without money — money flow is a veil over real flow (Classical view)

concepts.name: Circular Flow in the Context of India's National Income Estimation (CSO/MOSPI Methodology)
key_dimensions: India uses a combination of output and income methods; expenditure method is limited by data constraints
Base year revision (2011-12 series) changed methodology — GVA at basic prices replaced GDP at factor cost as primary measure
Informal/unorganised sector poses challenges — a large portion of India's circular flow is unrecorded
UPSC trap: GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + Product taxes – Product subsidies (not net indirect taxes in new methodology)

concepts.name: Circular Flow Disruptions: Structural Breaks and Economic Shocks
key_dimensions: Demand-side shocks (e.g., COVID lockdowns): consumption collapses → multiplier works in reverse → income contracts sharply
Supply-side shocks (e.g., oil price rise): production costs rise → stagflation — circular flow disrupted from the production side
Demonetisation as a case study: sudden liquidity withdrawal disrupted the money flow dimension of the circular flow
UPSC trap: Supply-side shocks cannot be resolved by demand-side (fiscal) stimulus alone — stagflation dilemma

concepts.name: Circular Flow and Sustainability: Green GDP and Environmental Leakages
key_dimensions: Conventional circular flow ignores environmental degradation — natural capital depletion is an unmeasured leakage
Green GDP / Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) attempts to adjust national income for environmental costs
SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) — UN framework for integrating environment into circular flow measurement
UPSC trap: Higher GDP can coexist with declining welfare if environmental degradation is severe — circular flow expansion ≠ development
